questions.q: Article 141 makes the Supreme Court's declared law binding, and Article 144 requires all civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Court. Analyse why the chapter needs both, and what each would fail to do on its own.
questions.a: The two articles act on different audiences and at different moments. Article 141 binds courts, and it binds them on the law: once the Supreme Court has declared what a rule means, every other court in the territory of India must apply that meaning, whether or not it was a party to the case. That is about the future and about reasoning. Article 144 reaches beyond courts to all civil authorities, and it is about a particular order actually taking effect. Article 141 alone would give the Court's rulings intellectual authority while leaving an individual order to be ignored by the officials who must carry it out -- a release ordered but no prisoner released. Article 144 alone would make each order effective while leaving every other court free to read the law differently next time, so the same question would be answered one way in one State and another way elsewhere, which would defeat the chapter's description of the Court as the final interpreter of the Constitution. Together they cover both what the law means everywhere and what happens in this case now.
s: Explains Article 141 as binding courts on the meaning of the law, for future cases
Explains Article 144 as reaching civil and judicial authorities so that an order is actually carried out
Shows what Article 141 alone would fail to do, such as an order nobody implements
Shows what Article 144 alone would fail to do, such as different courts reading the law differently

questions.q: 'Since Article 136 lets the Supreme Court take an appeal from any court or tribunal in India, the certificate requirement in Articles 132 and 133 is pointless.' Assess this.
questions.a: It is not pointless, because the two routes differ in who controls entry. Under Articles 132, 133 and 134A the High Court itself certifies that the case involves interpretation of the Constitution or a substantial question of law, and once it does, the appeal lies. Under Article 136 nothing lies as of right: the jurisdiction is extraordinary and discretionary, so the Supreme Court decides whether to grant leave at all. A certificate therefore gives a party something Article 136 cannot, namely a route that does not depend on the Supreme Court's discretion. The claim also ignores the grounds, which are stated differently in each. So the certificate route retains a clear purpose.
s: States that the certificate route gives an appeal once the High Court certifies, whereas Article 136 depends on the Supreme Court's discretion
Notes that Article 136 leave is extraordinary and discretionary, so nothing lies as of right
Concludes that the certificate route has a distinct purpose and rejects the claim

questions.q: Design a simple flowchart, described in words, that a Grade 8 student could use to work out which jurisdiction of the Supreme Court a given matter falls under. Use four decision points, name the article at each endpoint, and add one sentence on the limitation of your flowchart.
questions.a: A reasonable flowchart: Start by asking, is this a dispute between the Centre and a State, or between States? If yes, it is exclusive original jurisdiction under Article 131. If no, ask whether the President is seeking the Court's opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance. If yes, it is advisory jurisdiction under Article 143, heard by a Constitution Bench of not less than five judges. If no, ask whether a High Court has certified that the case involves interpretation of the Constitution or a substantial question of law, or whether it is a criminal case involving a death sentence. If yes, it is appellate jurisdiction under Articles 132, 133, 134 and 134A. If no, ask whether the party is seeking leave to appeal an order of any court or tribunal on a question of law of general public importance. If yes, it is Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136. Limitation: the chart leaves out writ jurisdiction under Article 32, which is a separate route for enforcing Fundamental Rights and does not fit this sequence of questions.
s: Builds four decision points in a workable order
Names the correct article at each endpoint, including 131, 143 and 136
Handles the appellate branch correctly, naming the High Court certificate or the death sentence route
States a genuine limitation, such as the omission of writ jurisdiction under Article 32

concepts.name: The High Courts
concepts.description: The highest court at the State level: Article 214 and why 28 States are served by 25 High Courts, which States and Union Territories share one, how High Court judges are appointed and qualified, when they retire, and the writ, appellate and supervisory powers a High Court exercises within its territorial limits.
concepts.idea: The Constitution promises a High Court to every State, but some States and Union Territories are small enough to share one, so the map of High Courts does not match the map of States.
concepts.rule: A High Court is the highest court at the State level, and Article 214 of the Constitution provides that there shall be a High Court in each State. At present India has 28 States, but there are 25 High Courts, since in some cases two or more States or Union Territories share a common High Court. A High Court consists of a Chief Justice and other Judges, and the number of judges varies from State to State. Judges of the High Court are appointed by the President of India in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court. Under Article 217(2) a High Court judge should be a citizen of India and must have held a judicial office in India, or been an advocate of a High Court or more than one High Court for ten years; High Court Judges retire at the age of sixty-two years under Article 217(1) and 224(3).
concepts.example: Each High Court exercises its powers within its territorial limits. It exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 226, entertains appeals against decisions of subordinate courts in civil and criminal matters as well as decisions of certain tribunals, and exercises supervisory control over all subordinate courts within its territorial limits. Under Article 227 every High Court has the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction -- a supervisory power, exercised to ensure they act within the bounds of their authority and jurisdiction, and to be exercised sparingly. The writ and supervisory jurisdiction of the High Courts has been declared to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

questions.q: Which article of the Constitution provides that there shall be a High Court in each State?
questions.a: Article 214

questions.q: At what age do High Court Judges retire, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Sixty-two years

questions.q: India has 28 States at present, but there are only ________ High Courts.
Under which article does every High Court have the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction?
questions.a: Article 227

questions.q: Why does India have fewer High Courts than States?
questions.a: In some cases two or more States or Union Territories share a common High Court
o: In some cases two or more States or Union Territories share a common High Court
Some States are too small to be allowed a court of their own
Three States have not yet had their High Courts established
Union Territories are not permitted to have any High Court

questions.q: Who is consulted by the President of India before a Judge of a High Court is appointed?
questions.a: The President appoints High Court Judges in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
s: Names the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State
Names the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court

questions.q: State the qualifications for appointment as a judge of a High Court under Article 217(2).
questions.a: The person should be a citizen of India, and must have held a judicial office in India, or have been an advocate of a High Court or more than one High Court for ten years.
s: States that the person should be a citizen of India
States that the person must have held a judicial office in India, or been an advocate of a High Court or more than one High Court for ten years

questions.q: Consider these statements about the High Courts. (I) The number of judges in a High Court varies from State to State. (II) Every High Court has the same Chief Justice, namely the Chief Justice of India. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Describe three things a High Court does within its territorial limits, as the chapter sets them out.
questions.a: It exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 226 for the violation of Fundamental Rights of citizens within the State. It entertains appeals against decisions of subordinate courts in civil and criminal matters, as well as decisions of certain tribunals. And it exercises supervisory control over the functioning of all subordinate courts within its territorial limits.
s: States that it exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 226
States that it entertains appeals against decisions of subordinate courts in civil and criminal matters, and of certain tribunals
States that it exercises supervisory control over the functioning of subordinate courts within its territorial limits

questions.q: A dispute arises in Puducherry. Which High Court does the chapter's table say covers it?
questions.a: Madras High Court

questions.q: Name the States and Union Territory covered by the Punjab & Haryana High Court, and give one other High Court from the table that covers more than one State or Union Territory.
questions.a: The Punjab & Haryana High Court covers Punjab, Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh. Another example is the Gauhati High Court, which covers Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh. Bombay, Calcutta, Kerala, Madras and the Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court are also acceptable.
s: Names Punjab, Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh
Names another multi-jurisdiction High Court from the table with what it covers

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true of the High Court's power of superintendence under Article 227?
questions.a: It allows the High Court to decide afresh any case pending before a subordinate court
o: It allows the High Court to decide afresh any case pending before a subordinate court
It extends over all courts and tribunals within the High Court's territorial jurisdiction
It is to be exercised sparingly

questions.q: An advocate who has practised in the Calcutta High Court for eleven years is proposed as a judge of that High Court. Assess her eligibility, and say how the requirement would differ if she were proposed for the Supreme Court.
questions.a: She is eligible for the High Court. Article 217(2) requires a citizen of India who has held a judicial office in India or has been an advocate of a High Court or more than one High Court for ten years, and eleven years of practice meets that. For the Supreme Court the advocate route also requires ten years as an Advocate of a High Court or more than one High Court, so she would meet that too; what differs is that the Supreme Court has two other routes -- five years as a Judge of a High Court, or being a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President -- while the High Court route in the chapter is judicial office in India or ten years at the Bar.
s: States that she is eligible under Article 217(2), citing the ten-year advocate requirement
States that the Supreme Court also has a ten-year advocate route, which she would meet
Identifies a real difference between the two sets of qualifications, such as the Supreme Court's five-year High Court judge route or the distinguished jurist route

questions.q: A subordinate court in a district begins deciding a type of case that no law allows it to hear. Which power of the High Court applies, how does the chapter describe it, and what limit does the chapter place on it?
questions.a: The power of superintendence under Article 227 applies. The chapter describes it as extending over all courts and tribunals within the High Court's territorial jurisdiction, as supervisory in nature, and as exercised to ensure that subordinate courts and tribunals act within the bounds of their authority and jurisdiction -- which is exactly what has gone wrong here. The limit the chapter places on it is that this power is to be exercised sparingly.
s: Identifies the power of superintendence under Article 227
Describes it as supervisory and as ensuring courts and tribunals act within the bounds of their authority and jurisdiction
States the limit: the power is to be exercised sparingly

questions.q: A student concludes from Article 214 that India must have exactly 28 High Courts, one for each State, and is confused by the figure of 25. Explain where her reasoning goes right, where it goes wrong, and give two examples from the table that settle it.
questions.a: She is right that Article 214 provides that there shall be a High Court in each State, and right that India at present has 28 States, so a reader who stopped there would expect 28. Where she goes wrong is in assuming that a High Court can serve only one State. The chapter says there are 25 High Courts because in some cases two or more States or Union Territories share a common High Court, so every State still has a High Court -- it is simply not always a separate one. Two examples from the table settle it: the Bombay High Court serves Maharashtra, Goa and the Union Territory of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, and the Gauhati High Court serves Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh. In both, several States are covered by a single court, which is how 28 States are served by 25 High Courts without Article 214 being broken.
s: Credits the correct part: Article 214 requires a High Court in each State and there are 28 States
Identifies the wrong assumption: that a High Court can serve only one State
States the chapter's explanation that two or more States or Union Territories share a common High Court
Gives two correct examples from the table with what each covers

questions.q: Assertion (A): India has fewer High Courts than it has States. Reason (R): Article 214 of the Constitution provides that there shall be a High Court in each State. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The chapter says the High Court's power of superintendence 'is to be exercised sparingly'. Analyse why a supervisory power would be limited in this way.
questions.a: Because the power is supervisory rather than appellate. The chapter says it exists to ensure that subordinate courts and tribunals act within the bounds of their authority and jurisdiction, which is a question about whether they were entitled to act at all, not about whether they decided rightly. If a High Court used it freely, it would in effect be re-deciding the work of the courts below, and the separate appeal route the chapter describes would become unnecessary. Used sparingly, it corrects a court that has stepped outside its authority while leaving the subordinate judiciary -- which the chapter calls a very important segment of the judicial system -- to do its own work.
s: States that the power is supervisory, concerned with whether a court acted within the bounds of its authority and jurisdiction
Explains that free use would turn it into re-deciding cases and duplicate the appeal route
Notes what sparing use preserves, such as the independence or importance of the subordinate judiciary

questions.q: The chapter notes in a single line that the writ and supervisory jurisdiction of the High Courts has been declared to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution. Analyse what those two jurisdictions do for an ordinary citizen, and why their loss would matter more than the loss of some other power.
questions.a: The writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is the citizen's own route into a High Court when her Fundamental Rights have been violated within the State -- it is how a right stops being a promise and becomes something a court will act on, and it is nearer and more reachable than travelling to the Supreme Court under Article 32. The supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 protects her from the other direction: it keeps the subordinate courts and tribunals she will actually appear before acting within the bounds of their authority and jurisdiction, so the court closest to her cannot exceed what it is entitled to do. Losing either would be worse than losing an ordinary power because between them they are what makes the rest of the system answerable at the State level. Without Article 226 a citizen's Fundamental Rights would be enforceable only at the apex, which for most people means not at all; without Article 227 the courts most people meet would have nobody watching them. That is a plausible reason for treating the two as more than ordinary provisions, though the chapter states the conclusion without explaining it.
s: Explains writ jurisdiction under Article 226 as the citizen's own route to enforce Fundamental Rights within the State
Notes that it is nearer and more reachable than Article 32 at the Supreme Court
Explains supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 as keeping the courts a citizen actually appears before within their authority
Argues why losing either would matter more than losing an ordinary power, for example that enforcement would exist only at the apex, or that local courts would go unwatched

questions.q: 'Because the number of judges varies from State to State, some States get worse justice than others.' Judge how far this chapter supports that conclusion.
questions.a: The chapter does not support it. It states only that the High Court consists of a Chief Justice and other Judges and that the number varies from State to State; it gives no figure for any High Court and offers no comparison of how well any of them work. Variation in numbers is not by itself evidence of worse justice, since States differ greatly in population and in how many cases arise. The chapter does, however, supply things that apply equally everywhere -- the same appointment process, the same Article 217 qualifications, the same retirement age and the same writ and supervisory jurisdiction -- which cut against the idea that some States have a weaker kind of High Court. The conclusion goes beyond the evidence in the chapter.
s: States that the chapter gives only the fact of variation, with no figures and no comparison of quality
Notes that varying numbers need not mean worse justice, since States differ in size and caseload
Points to features that are the same everywhere, such as appointment, qualifications, retirement age or jurisdiction

questions.q: Your class is making a wall map of India's High Courts. Write the instructions for the group, explaining how to colour the map so that a viewer can see at a glance why 28 States are served by 25 High Courts, and name four shared High Courts the map must label.
questions.a: A reasonable set of instructions: give every High Court its own colour, and shade each State or Union Territory in the colour of the High Court that covers it, rather than giving each State a colour of its own. A viewer will then see that most colours cover one State, but a few spread across several, and counting the colours rather than the shapes gives 25 rather than 28. Add a key listing each High Court beside its colour. The map must label at least four shared High Courts: Bombay High Court for Maharashtra, Goa and the Union Territory of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu; Gauhati High Court for Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh; Punjab & Haryana High Court for Punjab, Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh; and Kerala High Court for Kerala and the Union Territory of Lakshadweep. Calcutta, Madras and the Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court could be used instead. Finish with a caption saying that Article 214 provides for a High Court in each State, and that a State's High Court is not always a separate one.
s: Gives a colouring method that makes the sharing visible, such as one colour per High Court rather than per State
Explains how the method shows 25 rather than 28 to a viewer, and includes a key
Names four shared High Courts correctly with what each covers
Adds a caption or note referring to Article 214 and the fact that a State's High Court need not be a separate one

concepts.name: Subordinate Courts and tribunals
concepts.description: The courts below the High Courts -- District, Sessions, Revenue and Small Causes Courts, organised under Articles 233 to 237 -- and the specialised, quasi-judicial tribunals that decide particular categories of disputes, from consumer complaints to environmental and electricity matters.
concepts.idea: Most people never see the Supreme Court; the judiciary meets them in the district court down the road, or in a tribunal built for one kind of problem.
concepts.rule: In each State there is a system of subordinate courts below the High Courts. The Constitution makes a few provisions in Articles 233 to 237 to regulate the organisation of these courts and to ensure the independence of the subordinate judiciary. The subordinate judiciary constitutes a very important segment of the judicial system, as it is in these courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people. Subordinate Courts broadly include District Courts, Sessions Courts, Revenue Courts and Small Causes Courts. It is incumbent on each High Court to maintain and uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary in the concerned States, and the Governor of a State, in consultation with the High Court, appoints the District Judges under Article 233. Separately, there are specialised tribunals established under various enactments which are quasi-judicial in nature and decide on specific categories of disputes; a tribunal is a committee or body established to settle certain types of disputes.
concepts.example: The tribunals in Fig. 4.7 each have their own subject: Consumer Fora decide consumer disputes, the Central Administrative Tribunal decides service matters of Government employees, the National Green Tribunal decides environmental issues, the National Company Law Tribunal decides corporate civil commercial disputes including insolvency and bankruptcy, the Armed Forces Tribunal decides disputes related to the Armed Forces, and the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity decides electricity disputes. A family that had paid a builder an advance of almost Rs 65 lakh in 2011 and found no building four years later complained to the National Consumer Commission, which heard both parties and ordered the builder to return the amount with interest and to pay the cost of the litigation.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter list among the Subordinate Courts?
questions.a: Small Causes Courts

questions.q: Who appoints the District Judges, and in consultation with whom?
questions.a: The Governor of the State, in consultation with the High Court
o: The Governor of the State, in consultation with the High Court
The President of India, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India
The Chief Justice of India, in consultation with the Governor
The High Court, in consultation with the District Collector

questions.q: The Constitution makes provisions in Articles 233 to ________ to regulate the organisation of the subordinate courts and to ensure the independence of the subordinate judiciary.
Which tribunal does the chapter say decides service matters of Government employees?
questions.a: The Central Administrative Tribunal

questions.q: The chapter defines a tribunal as
questions.a: a committee or body established to settle certain types of disputes
o: a committee or body established to settle certain types of disputes
a court that hears appeals from the District Courts of a State
a bench of not less than five judges of the Supreme Court
a body that frames the rules under which courts function

questions.q: Why does the chapter call the subordinate judiciary a very important segment of the judicial system?
questions.a: Because it is in these courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people. They are the courts most people actually reach, so the subordinate judiciary is where the judicial system meets ordinary life.
s: States that it is in these courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people
Draws out why that matters, for example that these are the courts most people actually reach

questions.q: Match each of these tribunals to what it decides: the National Green Tribunal, the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, and Consumer Fora.
questions.a: The National Green Tribunal decides environmental issues; the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity decides electricity disputes; and Consumer Fora decide consumer disputes.
s: Matches the National Green Tribunal to environmental issues
Matches the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity to electricity disputes, and Consumer Fora to consumer disputes

questions.q: Consider these statements about tribunals. (I) They are quasi-judicial in nature. (II) They are established under various enactments. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Set out what the chapter says the Constitution and the High Courts each do for the subordinate judiciary.
questions.a: The Constitution makes a few provisions in Articles 233 to 237 to regulate the organisation of the subordinate courts and to ensure the independence of the subordinate judiciary. Each High Court has a duty of its own: it is incumbent on every High Court to maintain and uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary in the concerned States. The High Court also exercises supervisory control over the functioning of all subordinate courts within its territorial limits.
s: States that Articles 233 to 237 regulate the organisation of the subordinate courts and ensure the independence of the subordinate judiciary
States that it is incumbent on each High Court to maintain and uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary
Adds the High Court's supervisory control over subordinate courts within its territorial limits

questions.q: A company can no longer pay its debts and a corporate insolvency dispute arises. Which tribunal from Fig. 4.7 decides it?
questions.a: The National Company Law Tribunal

questions.q: A soldier has a dispute about his service in the army. Name the tribunal that would decide it, and one other tribunal from the chapter with the subject it handles.
questions.a: The Armed Forces Tribunal decides disputes related to the Armed Forces. Another example is the Central Administrative Tribunal, which decides service matters of Government employees. Any other tribunal from Fig. 4.7 with its correct subject is acceptable.
s: Names the Armed Forces Tribunal for disputes related to the Armed Forces
Names another tribunal from the chapter with the subject it handles

questions.q: Which of these is NOT named in the chapter as a kind of Subordinate Court?
questions.a: Family Courts

questions.q: Retell the builder case from the chapter and explain which forum decided it and what it ordered.
questions.a: A builder planned to start constructing a complex of flats in 2011, and a family decided to buy a flat and paid an advance of almost Rs 65 lakh. The family visited the site regularly and found that even after four years there was no sign of a building coming up, which was a breach of the agreement with the builder. The family went to the National Consumer Commission to complain. After listening to both parties, the Commission ordered the builder to return the amount to the family with interest, and also to pay the cost of the litigation.
s: Gives the facts: the 2011 plan, the advance of almost Rs 65 lakh, and no building after four years
States that this was a breach of the agreement and that the family complained to the National Consumer Commission
States the order: return the amount with interest, and pay the cost of the litigation

questions.q: Two disputes arise on the same day in a district: a neighbour has not repaid a small loan, and a factory is discharging effluents into a stream. Using the chapter, say which body each should go to and why the answers differ.
questions.a: The loan is an ordinary dispute with no specialised body attached to it, so it belongs to the subordinate courts in that district -- the courts in which, as the chapter says, the judiciary comes in close contact with the people. The effluents are an environmental issue, and the chapter says the National Green Tribunal decides environmental issues, so that dispute goes to a tribunal. The answers differ because tribunals are specialised, quasi-judicial bodies established under various enactments to decide specific categories of disputes, while the subordinate courts handle matters generally.
s: Sends the loan dispute to the subordinate courts in the district
Sends the effluents dispute to the National Green Tribunal, which decides environmental issues
Explains the difference: tribunals are specialised bodies for specific categories of disputes, while subordinate courts handle matters generally

questions.q: A relative says, 'Tribunals are just extra courts with a different name -- the country would be simpler with only District Courts, High Courts and the Supreme Court.' Using the chapter, set out what would be lost.
questions.a: What would be lost is specialisation. The chapter says tribunals are established under various enactments, are quasi-judicial in nature, and decide on specific categories of disputes -- each one is built for a single subject. Fig. 4.7 shows how narrow those subjects are: Consumer Fora for consumer disputes, the Central Administrative Tribunal for service matters of Government employees, the National Green Tribunal for environmental issues, the National Company Law Tribunal for corporate civil commercial disputes including insolvency and bankruptcy, the Armed Forces Tribunal for Armed Forces disputes, and the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity for electricity disputes. The builder case shows the practical value: a family that had paid almost Rs 65 lakh and seen no building took its complaint to the National Consumer Commission, which heard both parties and ordered the money returned with interest and the cost of the litigation. The relative is also wrong that tribunals stand outside the court system: the High Court's power of superintendence under Article 227 extends to all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction, and the Supreme Court hears appeals from tribunals such as the National Green Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. So tribunals are specialised bodies inside the structure, not duplicates of it.
s: States that tribunals are specialised, quasi-judicial bodies established under various enactments for specific categories of disputes
Gives at least three tribunals from Fig. 4.7 with the subject each decides
Uses the builder case or a similar example to show the practical value
Corrects the assumption that tribunals stand outside the system, citing Article 227 superintendence or appeals to the Supreme Court

questions.q: Assertion (A): The subordinate judiciary is a very important segment of the judicial system. Reason (R): Subordinate Courts include the Supreme Court and the High Courts, in addition to District and Sessions Courts. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The chapter says District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court, while High Court judges are appointed by the President in consultation with others. Analyse what the two appointment rules have in common.
questions.a: Both keep the appointment out of the hands of a single person and both require a judicial voice to be consulted. In each case the appointing authority is the constitutional head -- the Governor for the State, the President for the country -- and in each case a court must be consulted: the High Court for District Judges, and the Chief Justice of India together with the Governor and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court for High Court judges. The common pattern is a constitutional head appointing, with the judiciary consulted, which fits the chapter's concern with the independence of the judiciary.
s: Notes that in both cases the appointing authority is a constitutional head, the Governor or the President
Notes that in both cases a judicial authority must be consulted, naming at least one in each
Connects the pattern to judicial independence or to keeping the choice out of one person's hands

questions.q: Articles 233 to 237 are said to regulate the organisation of the subordinate courts and 'to ensure independence of the subordinate judiciary'. Analyse why independence needs protecting at this level in particular, using what the chapter says about these courts.
questions.a: Independence matters most where power is closest and least visible. The chapter says it is in the subordinate courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people, which means these are the courts that decide the great majority of ordinary disputes and the ones most citizens will ever appear before. A district judge also works within the State, among the very officials and interests whose disputes he may have to decide, so the pressure on him is nearer at hand than it is on a judge in New Delhi. That is why the Constitution does not leave the matter to State administration alone: Articles 233 to 237 regulate the organisation of these courts, the appointment of District Judges under Article 233 requires the Governor to consult the High Court rather than deciding alone, and it is made incumbent on each High Court to maintain and uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary. At the same time the High Court's power of superintendence under Article 227 is to be exercised sparingly, so supervision does not become control. The design protects these courts from the executive without handing them over to the court above.
s: Explains that these are the courts that come in close contact with the people and decide most ordinary disputes
Argues that pressure is nearer at hand at this level, or that these courts are less visible than the higher ones
Names concrete protections, such as Articles 233 to 237, the consultation requirement under Article 233, or the High Court's duty to uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary
Notes the balance, for example that Article 227 superintendence is to be exercised sparingly so supervision does not become control

questions.q: 'The builder case proves that ordinary people can win against powerful parties.' Assess how much weight this one example can carry.
questions.a: It carries real but limited weight. On the positive side, the case is exactly what it is said to be: a family that had paid an advance of almost Rs 65 lakh recovered it with interest and the cost of the litigation from a builder, after the National Consumer Commission heard both parties. That shows the forum works and that being the smaller party is not fatal. But one reported example cannot prove a general rule. The chapter gives no figures for how often such complaints succeed, says nothing about families who could not afford to pursue a case at all, and even withholds the parties' names, so nothing further can be checked. It is a fair illustration of what a tribunal can do, not proof of what usually happens.
s: Credits what the example does show, citing the order to return the amount with interest and the cost of the litigation
Notes that a single example cannot establish a general rule
Identifies what the chapter does not supply, such as success rates, the position of those who cannot pursue a case, or the withheld names

questions.q: Design a simple help-desk card for your local area titled 'Where should this dispute go?'. Write six entries, each naming a kind of problem and the court or tribunal for it, and add one line telling a reader what to do when none of the six fits.
questions.a: A reasonable card: (1) A shop sold you a faulty item and will not replace it -- Consumer Fora, which decide consumer disputes. (2) A Government employee has a dispute about her service -- the Central Administrative Tribunal. (3) A factory is polluting the air or water -- the National Green Tribunal, which decides environmental issues. (4) A company cannot pay its debts, or a corporate commercial dispute has arisen -- the National Company Law Tribunal, which also handles insolvency and bankruptcy. (5) A dispute about service in the Armed Forces -- the Armed Forces Tribunal. (6) A dispute with an electricity provider -- the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity. Closing line: if none of these fits, take the matter to the subordinate courts in your district -- the District, Sessions, Revenue or Small Causes Courts -- since tribunals exist only for specific categories of disputes and the ordinary courts handle the rest.
s: Writes six entries, each pairing a realistic problem with a body from the chapter
Matches every tribunal to the subject the chapter actually gives it
Closes by directing an unmatched dispute to the subordinate courts, and explains why

concepts.name: A faster and more accessible justice system: new laws, digital access and alternate dispute resolution
concepts.description: How the justice system is being made quicker and easier to reach -- the three criminal laws replaced in 2023, the digital initiatives from e-Filing to the Virtual Justice Clock, and the alternate modes of dispute resolution: arbitration, mediation, Lok Adalats and Gram Nyayalayas.
concepts.idea: Justice delayed or out of reach is barely justice at all, so the system is being changed in three directions at once -- newer laws, an open digital front door, and routes that settle a dispute without a full court case.
concepts.rule: Three colonial-era laws were replaced in 2023: the Indian Penal Code, 1860 by the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. These laws aim to facilitate faster justice, the use of digital evidence, and better protection for victims, while making the justice system modern, transparent and effective. Digital technology has been introduced to make the judicial system more accessible and transparent: litigants can directly check the details of their cases instead of only relying on their lawyers, and copies of court orders and judgements are freely available to the public in multiple languages. To further strengthen the system and reduce the burden on the judiciary, courts increasingly encourage litigants to settle disputes through alternate modes of dispute resolution such as arbitration, mediation or conciliation, negotiation and Lok Adalat.
concepts.example: In arbitration the parties refer their dispute to an arbitrator or panel of arbitrators -- a retired judge, a lawyer or an expert -- who must act fairly and impartially and let each party put forth its case; the decision is final, legally binding and enforceable by a court of law, under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. In mediation, the most common form of ADR, a neutral Mediator assists the parties to a mutual settlement but has no power to decide or impose a view, under The Mediation Act, 2023. Lok Adalats, recognised under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, function as people's courts that settle disputes amicably and reduce judicial backlog; and Gram Nyayalayas, under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, are mobile, village-level courts using a simplified procedure with no technicalities.

questions.q: Two families in a village have quarrelled over a boundary and want it settled amicably, without the formality of a court. Using the chapter, name two routes open to them and say what each offers.
questions.a: A Lok Adalat is one route: it is a special forum where disputes can be settled or resolved amicably, it functions as a people's court, and it works without the rigours of formal adjudication. The chapter also says that in some cases parties can approach a Lok Adalat even before going to Court. Mediation is a second route: a neutral Mediator assists the parties in arriving at a mutual settlement and has no power to impose a view, so the families keep control of the outcome. A Gram Nyayalaya would also be acceptable, being a mobile, village-level court with a simplified procedure and no technicalities.

questions.q: A dispute could be sent to arbitration or to mediation. Explain how you would choose between them, setting out what each involves and what each cannot give the parties.
questions.a: The choice turns on whether the parties want someone to decide for them or only to help them agree. In arbitration the parties refer the dispute to an independent adjudicator or panel called an arbitrator, who may be a retired judge, a lawyer or an expert. The arbitrator must act fairly and impartially and allow each party to put forth its case, and the decision is final, legally binding on the parties and enforceable by a court of law, under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. What arbitration cannot give is an outcome both sides have chosen: someone loses, and is bound. In mediation, the most common form of ADR, a neutral person appointed as Mediator assists the parties in arriving at a mutual settlement under The Mediation Act, 2023. The mediator has no power to make any decision or impose a view, so the parties keep control. What mediation cannot give is a guaranteed end: if the parties do not agree, nothing binds them. So arbitration suits parties who need certainty and expert judgement on a technical question; mediation suits parties who must continue dealing with each other and would rather settle than be ruled against.
s: Describes arbitration accurately, including who the arbitrator may be and that the decision is final, binding and enforceable
Describes mediation accurately, including the neutral mediator, the mutual settlement, and the absence of any power to decide or impose
States what each cannot give: no chosen outcome in arbitration, no guaranteed end in mediation
Reaches a reasoned choice, matching each mode to the kind of parties or dispute it suits

questions.q: The chapter says copies of court orders and judgements are made freely available to the public in multiple languages. Analyse why the words 'freely' and 'in multiple languages' each matter.
questions.a: 'Freely' removes cost as a barrier: a judgment that must be paid for is open only to those who can pay, so making copies free extends access beyond the parties and their lawyers to the public at large. 'In multiple languages' removes a second barrier, language, which cost alone would not touch -- a free judgment in a language a reader cannot follow is still closed to her. The chapter's own reason covers both: this is done so that anyone can read and understand the proceedings of the court, and understanding needs the document to be both obtainable and readable. Together the two words are what turn transparency from a claim into something a citizen can actually use.
s: Explains that 'freely' removes cost as a barrier and extends access beyond the parties
Explains that 'in multiple languages' removes the separate barrier of language
Cites the chapter's purpose that anyone can read and understand the proceedings of the court, needing both

questions.q: The chapter's closing pages push in three directions at once -- new criminal laws, digital initiatives, and alternate modes of dispute resolution. Analyse what single problem all three are addressing, and how each attacks a different part of it.
questions.a: All three address the same problem: a judicial system that handles a huge number of cases and is hard for an ordinary person to use, so that justice arrives slowly or not at all. The chapter names this when it says the judicial system addresses a huge number of cases on a regular basis, and when it introduces ADR as a way to reduce the burden on the judiciary. Each direction attacks a different part. The new laws of 2023 work on the rules themselves: they aim to facilitate faster justice, the use of digital evidence and better protection for victims, making the system modern, transparent and effective -- that is, the law a case is decided under. The digital initiatives work on access and visibility: e-Filing, hybrid hearings, live streaming, translation of judgments and the National Judicial Data Grid let a litigant check her own case instead of depending entirely on her lawyer and let the public read judgments freely and in multiple languages, while the Virtual Justice Clock puts real time judicial data at the Court's own gates. The alternate modes work on the volume: arbitration, mediation, Lok Adalats and Gram Nyayalayas resolve disputes without a full court case, which reduces backlog and, in the case of Gram Nyayalayas, decentralises justice to the village. Rules, access and volume are three separate causes of the same delay, which is why the chapter does not treat any one of them as sufficient.
s: Identifies the shared problem: a huge number of cases and a system hard for ordinary people to use, producing delay
Explains that the new laws work on the rules, citing faster justice, digital evidence or protection for victims
Explains that the digital initiatives work on access and transparency, with at least two concrete examples
Explains that the alternate modes work on volume and backlog, naming at least two of them

questions.q: 'Encouraging people to settle outside court weakens the judiciary, because fewer disputes are decided by judges.' Judge this against the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter takes the opposite view and gives reasons for it. It presents alternate modes as something courts themselves increasingly encourage, and as a way to further strengthen the judiciary and reduce its burden, so fewer cases is treated as relief rather than loss. Nor do these routes leave the courts behind: an arbitrator's award is enforceable by a court of law, Lok Adalats can resolve disputes already pending in the courts, and Gram Nyayalayas are courts themselves. The claim would have force only if settling outside court meant settling outside the law, and the chapter's examples are all statutory -- the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, The Mediation Act, 2023, the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 and the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008. On the chapter's account the judiciary is strengthened, not weakened.
s: States that the chapter presents ADR as encouraged by the courts themselves and as strengthening the judiciary while reducing its burden
Notes that these routes remain connected to the courts, for example that an award is enforceable by a court or that Lok Adalats resolve pending cases
Notes that each mode rests on a statute, so settling outside court is not settling outside the law

questions.q: Write a short speech of about ten sentences for your school assembly titled 'Justice you can actually reach', drawing on this part of the chapter. Use one change to the law, two digital initiatives and two alternate modes, and end with the chapter's point about what citizens themselves can do.
questions.a: A reasonable speech: Most of us picture justice as a courtroom we will never enter, and that picture is out of date. In 2023 three colonial-era laws were replaced -- among them the Indian Penal Code of 1860, now the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita -- with the aim of faster justice, the use of digital evidence and better protection for victims. Courts have also opened their doors digitally. A case can now be filed electronically through e-Filing, so a litigant does not have to travel to do it. Court proceedings are live streamed, and judgments are translated into multiple Indian languages and given free to the public, so anyone can read and understand what a court decided. Outside the courtroom there are quicker routes. A Lok Adalat is a people's court where a dispute can be settled amicably, without the rigours of formal adjudication, and in some cases people can go there even before going to court. A Gram Nyayalaya is a mobile, village-level court with a simplified procedure and no technicalities, created to bring justice nearer to where people live. None of this works, though, unless someone speaks up: the chapter reminds us that citizens have a role in helping the judicial system by bringing to its notice social concerns that affect the rights of people, animals and nature. Justice you can reach still needs someone willing to reach for it.
s: Names one change to the law accurately, with the old law and the new one
Names two digital initiatives from the chapter and says what each does for a citizen
Names two alternate modes accurately, such as Lok Adalats and Gram Nyayalayas
Ends with the chapter's point that citizens help by bringing social concerns affecting the rights of people, animals and nature to the judiciary's notice
